idiom_name: Thread::Queue + a fixed Thread pool, or concurrent-ruby FixedThreadPool / process-based workers
implementation_notes: The stdlib gives the queue and the primitives: Thread::Queue is a thread-safe FIFO with blocking pop that a fixed set of Threads pops from - the dispatcher is the queue plus the popping workers, and my own explicit hand-off loop only exists if the assignment must be decided. concurrent-ruby supplies the pool as a library object (a thread pool that reuses a fixed number of threads over a queue, plus executors, futures and supervisors), which is the form to use when you want bounds, shutdown and instrumentation rather than a hand-rolled loop. Since the GVL serializes Ruby bytecode, threads buy concurrency for I/O only; CPU-bound performers belong in processes (fork/Sidekiq-style workers), and the dispatcher then becomes a work distributor rather than a thread pool.
code_sketch:
q = Thread::Queue.new
done = Object.new                       # sentinel, not nil: messages may be nil
performers = 4.times.map do
  Thread.new do
    while (msg = q.pop) != done         # pop blocks until a message arrives
      handle(msg)                       # exactly one performer per message
    end
  end
end
channel.each { |msg| q << msg }
4.times { q << done }
performers.each(&:join)                 # join re-raises exceptions from the thread
pitfalls: The GVL means CPU-bound performers do not run in parallel; use processes (forks) for CPU work and keep threads for I/O.
Exceptions raised inside a Thread are invisible unless the thread is joined (or Thread.abort_on_exception is set): a silently dead performer shrinks the pool with no signal.
Thread::Queue#pop blocks forever when producers finish: a sentinel per worker (or #close) is required, and using nil as the sentinel breaks as soon as a legitimate message is nil.
An unbounded queue plus a fixed pool absorbs overload into memory; concurrent-ruby's fixed pool has the same unbounded queue unless you bound it at the producer.
Thread-local state (ActiveRecord connections and similar) must be established per thread and returned to the pool, or the first performer starves the rest.
